lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- A Glass of Barolo
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Julius Cesar do Nascimento | Lesson 8 -- A Glass of Barolo
lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses: defining and non-defining (who, which, whose, where, that)

listenings.text: My great-grandfather planted this vineyard in nineteen twenty-two, on a hill that faces the south. Four generations later, my brother and I still work on the same land. People ask me why our Barolo is special, and I always talk about the fog. Every autumn, a thick fog comes up from the river and covers the hills in the morning. It keeps the grapes cool. Nebbiolo is a grape that needs a long, slow season, and the fog gives it exactly that. Then comes the cellar. We don't sell anything young. Our Barolo stays in large wooden barrels for almost three years, and then it rests in the bottle. A good Barolo needs time. Years in the cellar. If you open it too early, you only taste half of the story.

I write about wine for a living, so people often hand me the wine list at business dinners, which can be a lot of pressure. Here's my method. First, I look for the region and the vintage, because they tell me most of what I need to know. Then I think about the food, not about my own taste. If I don't know any of the wines, I'm not embarrassed. I simply ask the sommelier for a wine that pairs with what we're eating, and I give a price range. Sommeliers love that question. And one rule I never break at a business dinner: I never choose the most expensive bottle. It looks like you're trying too hard, and your host may feel uncomfortable.

I make wine in the Barossa Valley, in South Australia, which is famous all over the world for Shiraz. Our wines are big, warm and full-bodied, like the weather. When I was twenty-five, I spent one year working in a small winery in Piedmont, in Italy, and it changed the way I think. In Australia, we were always in a hurry. Pick the grapes, make the wine, sell it the next year. The family that I worked for had wines in their cellar that were fifteen years old. The old man, whose name was Giuseppe, used to say that wine is like a person. It needs time to become itself. That year, I learned patience. Now I let my best wines age, and I don't sell them too early.

paras: I had been to Italy many times for work, but I had never visited a winery. So when our Italian partner, who is a wine lover, invited me to Piedmont after a meeting in Turin, I said yes immediately. We drove for an hour into the hills, where the vineyards cover every slope like green stripes. It was the end of the harvest, and the air smelled of grapes.

The winemaker, Marco, whose great-grandfather had planted the first vines, met us at the door. He took us down to the cellar, which was cold, dark and very quiet. Hundreds of large wooden barrels were waiting there. “This is the wine that we will sell in four years,” Marco said. “Barolo, which is made only from the Nebbiolo grape, needs time. If you open it too young, it is hard and closed.”

At dinner, Marco opened a 2016 vintage. It was full-bodied, but elegant, with a smell of roses and cherries. He paired it with a simple risotto, and it was perfect. I took a sip, looked at the label and asked him how many bottles I could take home in my suitcase. The answer was six. Since that evening, every time I see a Barolo on a wine list, I think of that cold, quiet cellar and of the people who wait years for one glass.
